analysis.one_liner: Limits courts' power to keep health and safety hazards secret in lawsuit settlements.
analysis.headline: The bill to curb secret settlements held one hearing, then died in House committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Companies often settle lawsuits on condition that the evidence stays sealed, so courts and the public never learn about a dangerous drug, a defective product, or a workplace hazard. This bill would have barred federal courts from approving such secrecy unless the judge first found, on the record, that no public health or safety hazard was being hidden, or that a specific and substantial confidentiality interest outweighed the public's interest in disclosure. It would also have let parties report hazards to regulators and talk publicly about settlement terms other than the money paid. The bill never advanced past committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers, patients, and workers, who would learn about health and safety hazards uncovered in court cases instead of having that evidence buried under a settlement's confidentiality terms; also journalists, regulators, and future plaintiffs who could use the information to avoid or expose dangerous products.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers, patients, and workers exposed to hazards

how_it_helps.text: Courts could not enter protective orders, approve settlements that restrict disclosure of discovery information, or seal court records unless the judge first found the order would not restrict disclosure of information relevant to public health or safety, or that a specific and substantial confidentiality interest outweighed the public interest in disclosure of potential hazards [S2].
The party seeking secrecy would bear the burden of proof, protective orders could be no broader than necessary, and the public-interest finding would have to be renewed after final judgment [S3].
No party could demand, as a condition of producing evidence, that the other side agree to a secrecy order that violates the Act, closing a common negotiation tactic [S2].

Courts could not enforce settlement terms forbidding a party from reporting information to federal or state agencies that regulate the activity, or from disclosing that a settlement was reached or its terms other than the money paid [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Companies facing product-liability and other civil suits would lose the ability to buy confidentiality that keeps hazard evidence out of public view, and parties with genuinely sensitive information would face a heavier showing and more litigation before a judge approves secrecy. The bill did carve out a presumption protecting individuals' personal financial and health information, and expressly left classified information untouched.
analysis.who_pays_short: Companies that buy secrecy in settlements

drawbacks.text: Business information with no health or safety dimension would still need court findings to stay sealed, meaning more hearings, added litigation expense, and possibly slower settlements for defendants with legitimate trade secrets [S3].

The bill requires a judge to weigh the public interest in disclosure against confidentiality interests case by case, which invites contested litigation over what counts as a potential health or safety hazard in every sealing request [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real and hard to replace: evidence of dangerous products and drugs now surfaces in lawsuits and is routinely buried, and no other mechanism forces it into the open. The costs are procedural rather than substantive — more motions and findings around protective orders — and the bill already protects personal privacy with a presumption favoring individuals' financial and health information, while leaving classified information alone. On balance the design is targeted, though the added litigation burden on ordinary civil cases is a fair objection.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Judiciary Committee, got a subcommittee hearing in June 2009, was shifted to a different subcommittee in May 2010, and never reached a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Robert Wexler of Florida, joined by Rep. Jerrold Nadler and three Democratic cosponsors, introduced the bill on March 12, 2009, and it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee [S1].
On May 29, 2009 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Commercial and Administrative Law, which held a hearing on June 4, 2009 [S5].
On May 29, 2010, the bill was referred to a different subcommittee, the Subcommittee on Courts and Competition Policy, and no markup or floor vote ever followed [S5].
With only three cosponsors and no committee vote, the bill died when the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011 [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that settle lawsuits under seal came out ahead, since the evidence of health and safety hazards in their files stays buried, and the House Judiciary Committee leadership avoided the fight entirely.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Companies that settle lawsuits under seal

for.name: Rep. Robert Wexler
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Sunshine in Litigation Act and shepherded it through an initial subcommittee referral.

for.name: Rep. Jerrold Nadler
for.what_they_did: Joined Wexler in introducing the bill.

for.name: Subcommittee on Commercial and Administrative Law
for.what_they_did: Held a hearing on the bill on June 4, 2009, the only consideration it received.

against.name: Chair John Conyers
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill before the full committee for a markup or sent it to the floor; after one subcommittee hearing it was moved to another subcommittee and stalled there.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; the sponsor and all three cosponsors were Democrats, and no Republican support appears in the record.

industries.note: These companies rely on confidential settlements to keep evidence of defective products and unsafe drugs out of public view. The bill would have stripped judges' authority to enforce that secrecy when public health or safety is implicated, letting regulators and the public see what the litigation uncovered.
